name: Omar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the complaints row for a small heating-service contact centre called Warmline. The difficult calls come to me when an engineer's visit has been missed or a tenant has no heat. I have a two-year college diploma and know the complaint rules cold, but the company pays its team leads less than the bigger centres do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when a complaint reaches you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the work order and phone the engineer before I promise a new visit. Sometimes an AI draft helps me find the right clause, but I do not let it tell a cold household to be patient without checking. My partner Leena's hours at a laundry shift change week by week, and we have only three weeks of expenses saved.

I would ask for **paid checking time** before closing hard cases.

feel: **Anxious** about current household costs despite mild AI.

steps.text: Keep paid lead complaint shifts and call engineers before closing missed-visit cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little AI shortcuts won't replace a call to the engineer. If a boiler is cold, the family wants a visit date, not a clever paragraph. I'd keep asking management for enough paid time to check the hard complaints properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe my lead work survives the mild version, but three weeks saved leaves us exposed even with no AI surprise. Leena's laundry shifts can be short, and my wage already barely covers our rent and utilities. I don't know what income would replace mine if I stopped working later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the escalated heating complaints and calling engineers before closing a case. This year Leena and I would put our rent, utilities and actual weekly pay on a sheet and stop the small monthly games subscription. In the first year of this picture I'd keep the paid lead rota and put that saved subscription money toward a fourth week of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money, though the technology picture itself is quiet. One missed laundry shift can leave us counting days. I can at least make the costs visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that spending cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The games subscription is the easiest small cut. It will not fix the whole gap, but it buys a little room. We are not counting our grown children's wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being near retirement make the quiet scenario safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead title does not turn three weeks of savings into a comfortable retirement. I would ask for written figures about any later income before deciding on fewer hours. Until then, I plan to keep earning.

say: I would ask for **paid human review** of missed heating visits.
I would bring **documented errors** with the complaints row to the union.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink even if the title survives.
I see few **nearby paid roles** if Warmline cuts complaints.
do: Log **wrong visit promises** against engineer rotas while taking paid calls.
Join four agents in a **union request** for written paid checking hours.
Cancel the **monthly daughter visit** only if my paid hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about rent exposure, with a group plan for errors.
S1.quote: A wrong visit promise can leave a family in a cold house.
fieldNote: His concern is **hours lost** before formal redundancy.
The union request involves **five workers**, including Omar.
The daughter visit changes only after **actual pay loss**, without asking her for funds.

steps.text: Keep paid complaints calls and log generated visit promises against engineer rotas
Join four other agents asking union branch for written paid checking and reopening time
Cancel monthly coach trip to daughter only if Omar’s paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that automatic complaint answers can save time, but someone must check a missed heating visit before closing it. Five of us on the complaints row would ask the union branch together for paid human-review time. We should show actual cases, not just argue about whether a tool is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company could let routine complaint calls go and squeeze the hours of the people left. My lead skill may help for a while, but I do not see a new post in this small town if Warmline cuts the row. Three weeks saved makes a reduction in pay serious before anyone loses a whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep a log of generated answers that promise visits no engineer accepted. I'd join the other four complaints agents in a union request for written paid checking hours and a way to reopen wrong answers. If my own paid hours fall over the next few years, Leena and I would cancel the monthly coach trip to visit our daughter and use calls instead; in the first year I'd keep all available shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because fewer paid hours would hit our rent. I can still gather evidence and work with the group. I do not want fear to become a reason to send customers bad information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group bring to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put dates, customer consent and the engineer's actual rota beside each wrong answer. A wrong visit promise can leave a family in a cold house. The union branch can ask as a group for a paid process to fix those errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would call our daughter instead of visiting each month only if my payslip shows fewer hours. I would not ask her for money. A visit is lovely, but the rent is due first.

fieldNote: He expects to lose the **lead row**, not merely routine tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coworkers that full AGI could handle complaint notes and customer replies by 2028; robots around 2031 do not delay a headset cut. We should demand written closure dates and the hours we can still be paid for. I don't want a manager saying there are jobs somewhere without naming a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Warmline to close most of my complaints row in the first year after 2028, and I'd be awake at night over the rent. Three weeks saved will not carry us through a long search. Leena's variable laundry pay cannot replace my wage, and the few nearby centres may cut too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join the complaints row in asking the union branch for written closure and paid-hour dates. I'd check posted paid counter roles at the repair depot and the one local clinic by complete weekly wages, hours and bus cost. If my row ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a posted paid opening; I would accept only a rota whose full weekly wage and hours after travel cover rent and utilities, while taking any remaining Warmline calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would expect a big income loss and would be awake adding up bus fares and rent. The plan is small because the local job list is small, but it is a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can Leena's work cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena would keep taking laundry shifts that are paid, but I cannot use a good week as the monthly figure. We would write down several weeks of actual pay. Our grown children have their own rent, so I would not count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the depot counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot counter deals with parts handed over to a customer, which may last a little longer than a phone queue. I would check the posted duties and safe handling before taking it. Robots around 2031 could change that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to argue for paid complaint-review work before the desk is cut. We should ask Warmline to post actual positions and show their weekly hours. A job title cannot heat a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach newer agents how to verify an engineer's visit, and that might keep some paid hours through 2031. I still think cheap thinking AI could close our complaints queue. If I have to move, I need a real wage before calling any nearby desk a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd write a short guide from real missed-visit cases and ask the supervisor to give me paid time to teach it in team meetings. I'd keep my lead calls while they pay and join the four other agents in asking the union for any posted paid review jobs and their hours. In the first year after 2031, if my queue closes, I'd apply to a posted local counter only if its weekly wage and hours after bus fares cover rent and utilities; otherwise I'd keep available paid calls and search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years is useful, but it is not a wage, and our savings still cover only weeks. I would feel better teaching something that prevents a cold night, not collecting a certificate nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you teach the newer agents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use three actual missed visits from my log and show what question the draft answer missed. If the supervisor will not pay for teaching time, I will keep that guide for myself, not work extra unpaid shifts. My own rent needs a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no review post appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid Warmline calls while any exist and check the posted roles again. Leena and I would hold the subscription saving as cash. We would not assume the union could create a new employer in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives workers time to ask for honest pay and staffing plans each year. The thinking work on my headset can still change by 2036, before robots reach physical tasks around 2039. I would rather have written rotas than a retirement slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may still need a wage because we have not verified any income that would replace it. Three weeks saved is an urgent problem now, not a plan for later. I could spend a decade checking rosters and still arrive with no cushion unless we set aside something each payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Leena and I would keep the subscription money in a separate rent reserve and check written figures for any later-life income. I'd stay on the paid complaints rota while it exists and ask the union branch with the team for annual staffing dates. If calls end in the first year after 2036, I'd apply to a posted paid counter role only if full-week wages and hours after travel cover rent and utilities; if verified later income remains too small, I'd continue seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, despite the long warning. Rent is due next month and savings cover only weeks. Ten years gives time to build a cushion if the pay allows, but it doesn't settle today's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the reserve grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the weekly pay can spare it, we will add a little from each payday to the rent reserve. If a laundry week is short, we will keep the rent current rather than pretend the saving target is fixed. I won't call a thin bank account retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our grown children are welcome to visit, but they have their own bills. I would show them our plan if they asked, not put their earnings on our sheet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most because the complaints row could go before we can build more than three weeks of rent money. Written closure dates and a real paid opening close enough for the bus would help. I would also need the paid hours written down, not a course promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what it costs to keep a household warm while a complaint waits. My own rent does not pause because the employer calls me a team lead. I want fewer speeches and more paid hours.

headlineQuote: My own rent does not pause because the employer calls me a team lead.
portrait: Omar is a **58-year-old** complaint-row lead with a two-year college diploma.
He has **three weeks saved**, lower pay and few nearby centres despite high skill.
He uses AI **occasionally** but checks engineer visits before making promises.
He joins colleagues for **written paid hours** while guarding rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when a quick complaint-row closure could outrun three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Written **closure dates**, paid hours and reachable posted jobs.
